name: argumentation_schemes
description: Walton-style defeasible argumentation schemes — the recurring inference patterns of everyday, legal, and scientific reasoning — each with the critical questions that test its use.

source_based.name: argument from expert opinion
source_based.definition: Source E is an expert in domain D, E asserts that A is true (or false) within D, therefore A may plausibly be taken as true.
critical_questions: How credible is E as an expert source?
Is E an expert in the field that A actually falls in?
What did E assert, exactly, and does it entail A?
Is E personally reliable and free of conflicting interest?
Is A consistent with what other experts assert, and is it backed by evidence?
source_based.example: The bridge inspector, a licensed structural engineer, says the deck has lost load capacity; so it probably has.
source_based.caution: Slides into the appeal-to-authority fallacy when the field is mismatched, the assertion is paraphrased loosely, or dissent is hidden.

source_based.name: argument from position to know
source_based.definition: Source S is in a position to know about things in a certain domain and asserts that A is true in that domain, therefore A is plausibly true.
critical_questions: Is S really in a position to know whether A holds?
Is S honest, and does S have a stake in the answer?
Did S actually assert A rather than something weaker?
source_based.example: The night shift supervisor was on the floor when the alarm sounded, and she says no one entered the vault.

source_based.name: argument from witness testimony
source_based.definition: Witness W was in a position to observe event A, W testifies that A occurred, therefore A occurred.
critical_questions: Was W in a position to observe the event, under what conditions?
Is W's testimony internally consistent and consistent with the known facts?
Does W have a bias, interest, or motive to shade the account?
How reliable is memory of this kind of event after this much time?
source_based.example: Two tellers testify that the man at the counter wore no mask.
source_based.caution: Confidence in eyewitness testimony correlates weakly with accuracy; treat vividness as no evidence of reliability.

source_based.name: argument from corroborative testimony
source_based.definition: Two or more independent sources assert A, therefore A is more plausible than either source alone would make it.
critical_questions: Are the sources genuinely independent, or do they share an origin?
Could the agreement be explained by contagion, collusion, or a common rumor?
Do the accounts agree on the load-bearing detail or only the periphery?
source_based.example: Three vendors who never met each other describe the same defect in the same batch.

source_based.name: argument from expert consensus
source_based.definition: The relevant expert community has converged on A through its own review procedures, therefore A is plausibly true.
critical_questions: Is the convergence real, or is it manufactured by a single funder, journal, or school?
Was the consensus reached by independent replication or by deference?
How does the consensus handle its best-documented anomalies?
source_based.example: Every major statistical agency computes the series the same way, so the definition is not idiosyncratic.
source_based.aka: argument from convergence of expert opinion

source_based.name: argument from popular opinion
source_based.definition: A is generally accepted as true, therefore there is a presumption in favor of A.
critical_questions: Is A really generally accepted, or is that an impression from one's own circle?
Is there reason to think the many are in a position to know?
Is there specific evidence that outweighs the presumption?
source_based.example: Nearly every experienced sailor treats that channel as unsafe at low tide; that is at least a reason to check.
source_based.caution: Legitimate only as a weak presumption; treated as proof it becomes the ad populum fallacy.

source_based.name: argument from popular practice
source_based.definition: A course of action is what most people in a group actually do, therefore it is prudentially or normatively acceptable for a member of that group.
critical_questions: Is the practice really widespread in the relevant group?
Does the practice reflect accumulated experience or mere convenience?
Are there known bad consequences the practice ignores?
source_based.example: Every yard in the trade double-checks the torque after a heat cycle, so we should too.

source_based.name: argument from common knowledge
source_based.definition: A is common knowledge in the relevant community, therefore A may be asserted without further support.
critical_questions: Is A actually common knowledge, or only assumed by the speaker?
Is the community whose knowledge is invoked the right one?
Has A been superseded since it became common?
source_based.example: Water boils lower on a mountain; no citation required.

source_based.name: argument from perception
source_based.definition: An agent perceives that A is the case under normal conditions, therefore A is the case.
critical_questions: Were the observing conditions normal — light, distance, attention, instrument calibration?
Is the perceptual claim a raw observation or an interpretation?
Is there a known illusion or artifact that produces this appearance?
source_based.example: The gauge reads zero pressure and the needle is not stuck; the line is empty.

source_based.name: argument from memory
source_based.definition: An agent recalls that A occurred, therefore A occurred.
critical_questions: How long ago, and how distinctive was the event?
Has the memory been rehearsed, suggested, or contaminated by later accounts?
Is there a contemporaneous record that agrees?
source_based.example: She remembers signing the form before the flood because she filed it that afternoon.

source_based.name: ethotic argument
source_based.definition: An arguer's demonstrated character — honesty, practical wisdom, goodwill — is offered as a reason to accept what the arguer says.
critical_questions: Is the character trait invoked relevant to the claim at hand?
Is the evidence of character actual conduct or self-presentation?
Does good character extend to competence in this domain?
source_based.example: He has reported his own errors twice before; when he says the number is wrong, it is worth a look.

source_based.name: argument from statement against interest
source_based.definition: A source asserts something that damages the source's own position, therefore the assertion is more credible than an interested one.
critical_questions: Does the statement really cut against the source's interest, all things considered?
Could the concession buy credibility for a larger claim?
Was the source aware the statement was damaging?
source_based.example: The company's own filing concedes the recall will cost a quarter of annual profit.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from cause to effect
causal_and_explanatory.definition: Generally, if A occurs then B will occur; A has occurred (or will), therefore B may be expected.
critical_questions: How strong is the causal generalization linking A to B?
Is the antecedent A actually established?
Are there interfering conditions in this case that would block B?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Cutting the subsidy raises the retail price; the subsidy was cut, so prices should rise.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from effect to cause
causal_and_explanatory.definition: B has been observed; A is the kind of thing that produces B; therefore A occurred.
critical_questions: Could B have been produced by something other than A?
How specific is B to A as a cause?
Is there independent evidence that A was present?
causal_and_explanatory.example: The scoring on the cylinder wall is what oil starvation does; the engine ran dry.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from correlation to causation
causal_and_explanatory.definition: A and B are statistically associated, therefore A causes B.
critical_questions: Is the correlation itself robust, or an artifact of sample or specification?
Could a third variable produce both A and B?
Could the causal direction run from B to A?
Is there a plausible mechanism and the right temporal order?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Districts that added tutoring saw scores rise faster, which is a reason — not yet a proof — that tutoring worked.
causal_and_explanatory.caution: The single most-abused scheme in popular argument; without design or mechanism it is a hypothesis, not a finding.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from sign
causal_and_explanatory.definition: A finding is taken as an indicator of a state of affairs, without any claim that the sign causes it.
critical_questions: How reliably does this sign accompany the state of affairs?
How often does the sign appear without it?
Are there other signs pointing the other way?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Frost heave in the pavement is a sign the drainage under it has failed.

causal_and_explanatory.name: abductive argument
causal_and_explanatory.definition: A body of facts is given; hypothesis H explains them better than the available alternatives; therefore H is plausibly true.
critical_questions: How well does H account for all the facts, not just the salient ones?
What are the rival hypotheses, and were they seriously considered?
How much better is H than the runner-up, and on what criteria?
What further evidence would discriminate between H and its rivals?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Only a leak upstream explains the pressure drop, the wet insulation, and the timing together.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from a causal mechanism
causal_and_explanatory.definition: A step-by-step process is identified by which A brings about B, therefore the causal claim is supported beyond mere association.
critical_questions: Is each step of the proposed mechanism independently evidenced?
Does the mechanism operate at the scale and dose in question?
Could the mechanism be real but too weak to produce the observed effect?
causal_and_explanatory.example: The additive binds the catalyst site, which is why conversion falls off after the second pass.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument to a common cause
causal_and_explanatory.definition: Two correlated phenomena are explained by positing a single antecedent cause of both, rather than a link between them.
critical_questions: Is the posited common cause independently observable?
Does it explain the timing and magnitude of both effects?
Would controlling for it make the association vanish?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Ice-cream sales and drownings both track summer heat.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from a counterfactual
causal_and_explanatory.definition: But for A, B would not have occurred; therefore A was a cause of B.
critical_questions: What is the comparison world, and is it specified precisely?
Would some other sufficient cause have produced B anyway (overdetermination)?
Is the counterfactual claim testable against any real comparison case?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Had the valve been replaced on schedule, the shutdown would not have happened.
causal_and_explanatory.caution: Counterfactual claims are cheap to assert and hard to check; demand the comparison case.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from a necessary condition
causal_and_explanatory.definition: B cannot occur without A; B occurred; therefore A was present (or: A is absent, therefore B cannot occur).
critical_questions: Is A genuinely necessary, or only usual?
Is the necessity a matter of definition, of physical law, or of institutional rule?
Are there documented cases of B without A?
causal_and_explanatory.example: No quorum, no valid vote; the vote is void.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from a sufficient condition
causal_and_explanatory.definition: A alone is enough to bring about B; A obtains; therefore B obtains.
critical_questions: Is A sufficient by itself, or only in combination with background conditions?
Are the background conditions satisfied here?
Is there a defeater that suspends the sufficiency in this case?
causal_and_explanatory.example: A single missing signature voids the filing, and one is missing.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from intervention
causal_and_explanatory.definition: Deliberately manipulating A changes B while everything else is held fixed, therefore A causes B.
critical_questions: Was the intervention on A only, or did it move other variables?
Was assignment to the intervention independent of the outcome?
Does the manipulated version of A resemble the real-world version?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Randomly assigned reminder letters raised filing rates by four points.

causal_and_explanatory.name: argument from dose-response gradient
causal_and_explanatory.definition: More of A is followed by more of B in an ordered way, therefore the association is more likely causal.
critical_questions: Is the gradient monotone, or read into noisy categories?
Could confounding also be graded across the same levels?
Is a threshold or saturating effect being forced into a linear story?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Each additional hour of exposure raised failure rates step by step.

causal_and_explanatory.name: causal slippery slope argument
causal_and_explanatory.definition: Taking the first step will set off a chain of causally linked consequences ending in an unacceptable outcome, therefore do not take the first step.
critical_questions: Is each link in the chain independently plausible?
What is the cumulative probability of the whole chain?
Is there a stopping point or control that breaks the chain?
causal_and_explanatory.example: Waiving the review for one project makes the waiver routine, and then the review is dead.
causal_and_explanatory.caution: Legitimate only when the intermediate links are argued; asserted as a chain it becomes the slippery-slope fallacy.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from analogy
analogy_and_classification.definition: Case C1 is similar to case C2 in relevant respects; A is true in C1; therefore A is true in C2.
critical_questions: Are the two cases similar in the respects that matter to the conclusion?
What are the relevant differences, and do they defeat the transfer?
Is there a third case similar to C1 in which A fails?
analogy_and_classification.example: Licensing drivers improved road safety, so licensing operators should improve site safety.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from precedent
analogy_and_classification.definition: A prior case was decided a certain way; the present case falls within the same rule or rationale; therefore decide it the same way.
critical_questions: Is the prior case actually governing, or merely persuasive?
Was the ruling on the point now at issue, or dictum?
Is there a material difference that distinguishes the present case?
analogy_and_classification.example: We granted the extension on identical facts last quarter.

analogy_and_classification.name: a fortiori argument
analogy_and_classification.definition: If the conclusion holds in a weaker case, then it holds all the more strongly in a stronger one.
critical_questions: Do both cases lie on the same scale of the relevant property?
Is the present case really 'more so' on that scale?
Could the conclusion have a ceiling that the stronger case exceeds?
analogy_and_classification.example: If a two-hour delay requires notice, a two-day delay certainly does.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from verbal classification
analogy_and_classification.definition: An item has a property that fits the classification term F, therefore the item can be classified as an F and treated accordingly.
critical_questions: Does the item really have the defining property?
Is the classification term being used in its standard sense?
Does classifying it as F actually carry the consequence claimed?
analogy_and_classification.example: The device stores and transmits health data, so it is a medical device under the rule.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from definition to verbal classification
analogy_and_classification.definition: A definition of F is offered, the item satisfies that definition, therefore the item is an F.
critical_questions: Is the definition the accepted one in this context?
Was the definition chosen to produce the desired classification?
Does the item satisfy every clause of the definition?
analogy_and_classification.example: A 'security' is an investment of money in a common enterprise with profits expected from others' efforts — and this is.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from vagueness of a verbal classification
analogy_and_classification.definition: A classification is too vague to apply reliably in this case, therefore the argument depending on it should not be accepted as it stands.
critical_questions: Is the term vague in a way that matters to the case at hand?
Could a stipulated definition resolve the vagueness fairly?
Is the vagueness objection being used to evade a clear central case?
analogy_and_classification.example: 'Reasonable notice' has no fixed meaning here, so the breach claim cannot rest on it alone.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from arbitrariness of a verbal classification
analogy_and_classification.definition: The classification draws a line at a point no better justified than nearby alternatives, therefore the classification should not carry the weight placed on it.
critical_questions: Is the line genuinely arbitrary, or defensible on administrability grounds?
Would any line do better, or is some line needed?
Does the case fall near the line or well inside it?
analogy_and_classification.example: Why is the cutoff fifty employees rather than forty-nine?

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from example
analogy_and_classification.definition: One or more instances of a kind are cited to support a general claim about that kind.
critical_questions: Is the example accurately described?
Is it typical of the class, or exceptional?
How many counter-instances are known?
analogy_and_classification.example: Two of the three plants that adopted the process cut waste in half.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from a paradigm case
analogy_and_classification.definition: A clear central instance fixes the meaning or standard for a term, and the disputed case is measured against it.
critical_questions: Is the case offered really paradigmatic for the community that uses the term?
Does the disputed case share the paradigm's essential features?
Has the paradigm shifted over time?
analogy_and_classification.example: If this is not a conflict of interest, nothing is.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from composition
analogy_and_classification.definition: Every part of a whole has property P, therefore the whole has property P.
critical_questions: Is P the kind of property that aggregates from parts to wholes?
Do interactions between the parts change the property?
Do all the parts really have P?
analogy_and_classification.example: Each stage of the process is reversible, so the whole process is reversible.
analogy_and_classification.caution: Valid only for additive or structure-independent properties; otherwise the fallacy of composition.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from division
analogy_and_classification.definition: A whole has property P, therefore its parts have property P.
critical_questions: Is P distributive over parts?
Is the part in question a typical part or a special one?
Does the whole have P only in virtue of arrangement?
analogy_and_classification.example: The fleet averages nine years old, so this aircraft is about nine years old.
analogy_and_classification.caution: Fails for emergent or averaged properties.

analogy_and_classification.name: argument from an established practice standard
analogy_and_classification.definition: The disputed conduct is classified by reference to what the recognized standard of the field requires.
critical_questions: Is the standard the recognized one, and current?
Does the standard actually cover this conduct?
Is the standard itself defensible, or merely customary?
analogy_and_classification.example: The inspection interval is set by the maintenance standard, and this interval was double it.

practical_and_value.name: practical reasoning
practical_and_value.definition: I have goal G; action A is a means to G; therefore I should do A.
critical_questions: Are there other means to G, and is A the best of them?
Is G a legitimate goal, and is it my most important one here?
Is A actually possible for me to carry out?
What are A's side effects, and do they outweigh G?
practical_and_value.example: We want the site open by March; only prefabrication gets us there; so prefabricate.

practical_and_value.name: value-based practical reasoning
practical_and_value.definition: Action A promotes a value V that the audience holds; therefore A should be done.
critical_questions: Does the audience actually hold V, or is it being imputed?
Does A really promote V rather than merely symbolize it?
Which competing values does A set back?
practical_and_value.example: Publishing the raw data serves transparency, which this institution says it values.

practical_and_value.name: argument from positive consequences
practical_and_value.definition: If A is brought about, good consequences will follow; therefore A should be brought about.
critical_questions: How likely are the good consequences?
Are they good by the audience's standards or only the speaker's?
What negative consequences accompany them?
practical_and_value.example: Moving the deadline gives every team a full test cycle.

practical_and_value.name: argument from negative consequences
practical_and_value.definition: If A is brought about, bad consequences will follow; therefore A should not be brought about.
critical_questions: How likely and how severe are the bad consequences?
Can they be mitigated rather than avoided by dropping A?
Are the consequences of not doing A worse?
practical_and_value.example: Cutting the maintenance window guarantees an unplanned outage later.

practical_and_value.name: argument from threat
practical_and_value.definition: If you do not accept A or do B, I (or my side) will bring about something bad for you.
critical_questions: Is the threatened consequence within the threatener's power?
Is the threat legitimate — a lawful sanction — or coercion?
Does the threat bear on the truth of A at all, or only on compliance?
practical_and_value.example: Miss the filing date and the license lapses by operation of law.
practical_and_value.caution: Legitimate as a warning about real sanctions; illegitimate when offered as a reason to believe rather than to act.

practical_and_value.name: argument from fear appeal
practical_and_value.definition: A frightening outcome is depicted, and a course of action is offered as the way to avoid it.
critical_questions: Is the depicted outcome realistic in probability and magnitude?
Is the recommended action actually effective against it?
Is fear doing work that evidence should be doing?
practical_and_value.example: Untreated, this corrodes to failure; replacing the section now avoids that.

practical_and_value.name: argument from danger appeal
practical_and_value.definition: A course of action carries a specific hazard to the audience, therefore avoid it.
critical_questions: Is the hazard documented for this situation?
Is the audience actually exposed to it?
Is the safer alternative genuinely safer overall?
practical_and_value.example: The ledge ices over after dusk; take the lower path.

practical_and_value.name: argument from need for help
practical_and_value.definition: Someone is in need, you are able to help at proportionate cost, therefore you should help.
critical_questions: Is the need real and as described?
Are you actually in a position to help effectively?
Does helping impose costs that fall on others?
practical_and_value.example: The clinic will close without a bridge grant, and the foundation has uncommitted funds.

practical_and_value.name: argument from distress
practical_and_value.definition: The suffering of a person or group is presented as itself a reason to act.
critical_questions: Is the distress accurately portrayed and representative?
Does the proposed action relieve it?
Is a single vivid case standing in for an unexamined general claim?
practical_and_value.example: Families are sleeping in cars two blocks from the empty units.
practical_and_value.caution: Slides into the appeal to pity when the distress is real but disconnected from the remedy proposed.

practical_and_value.name: argument from waste
practical_and_value.definition: Abandoning the course of action now would waste what has already been invested, therefore continue.
critical_questions: Are the past costs recoverable by continuing, or already sunk?
Judged from today, is completion still worth its remaining cost?
Is the waste framing masking an escalation of commitment?
practical_and_value.example: We are eighty percent through the migration; stopping strands the work.
practical_and_value.caution: Rational only when continuation has independent value or when partial work has salvage value.

practical_and_value.name: argument from sacrifice
practical_and_value.definition: Someone has borne a real cost for a cause, therefore the cause deserves support or the sacrifice deserves honoring.
critical_questions: Was the sacrifice made for the cause now invoked?
Does honoring it require this particular policy?
Is the sacrifice being used to foreclose criticism?
practical_and_value.example: The unit gave up its bonus pool to keep the line running through the recession.

practical_and_value.name: argument from alternatives
practical_and_value.definition: The options are A and B; B is unacceptable; therefore A.
critical_questions: Is the list of options exhaustive?
Is B genuinely unacceptable, or merely unattractive?
Could a combination or a modified option beat both?
practical_and_value.example: Either we shorten the scope or we slip the date; the date is contractual.
practical_and_value.caution: Collapses into the false dilemma when the option list is truncated.

practical_and_value.name: argument from opportunity cost
practical_and_value.definition: The resources A consumes have a better alternative use, therefore A should not be undertaken.
critical_questions: Is the alternative use actually available to these resources?
Is its return estimated on comparable terms?
Does A produce benefits the alternative cannot?
practical_and_value.example: The same crew-hours would clear the entire backlog of safety work.

practical_and_value.name: argument from precaution
practical_and_value.definition: The potential harm is severe and irreversible and the science is unsettled, therefore act to prevent it before proof arrives.
critical_questions: Is the harm both plausible and irreversible?
Is the precaution itself free of comparable harms?
What evidence would end the uncertainty, and how fast can it be got?
practical_and_value.example: Stop the discharge while the groundwater tests run.
practical_and_value.caution: Symmetric application matters: inaction has risks too, and precaution can be invoked on both sides.

practical_and_value.name: argument from a value hierarchy
practical_and_value.definition: Two goods conflict; one is ranked above the other in a hierarchy the audience accepts; therefore prefer the higher.
critical_questions: Is the ranking one the audience actually endorses?
Is the conflict genuine, or can both be served?
Is the ranking context-dependent in a way that reverses it here?
practical_and_value.example: Safety outranks schedule in this organization's stated order of priorities.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from an established rule
rule_and_precedent.definition: A rule requires that in circumstances C, action A be taken; C obtains; therefore A must be taken.
critical_questions: Is the rule in force and applicable to this actor?
Do the present circumstances actually satisfy C?
Is there a recognized exception that applies?
rule_and_precedent.example: Filings over the threshold require board approval, and this one is over.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from an exceptional case
rule_and_precedent.definition: The case falls under the rule's letter but within a recognized exception, therefore the rule's normal consequence does not follow.
critical_questions: Is the exception recognized, or invented for the occasion?
Does this case fall within the exception's own conditions?
Would the exception swallow the rule if generalized?
rule_and_precedent.example: Emergency repairs are exempt from the pre-approval requirement.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from plain meaning
rule_and_precedent.definition: The text's ordinary meaning settles the question, therefore no further interpretation is needed.
critical_questions: Is the meaning plain to the relevant readership, or only to the speaker?
Is there a term of art that displaces ordinary usage?
Does the plain reading produce an absurd result?
rule_and_precedent.example: 'Any vehicle' includes bicycles unless the code defines otherwise.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from legislative purpose
rule_and_precedent.definition: The rule was adopted to achieve a purpose; the reading that serves that purpose should be preferred.
critical_questions: Is the purpose evidenced in the text or record, or reconstructed?
Was there one purpose or a compromise among several?
Does the purposive reading stretch the text past what it can bear?
rule_and_precedent.example: The notice period exists so tenants can find housing; a weekend-only notice defeats it.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument for a constitutive rule
rule_and_precedent.definition: An institutional fact holds because a rule constitutes it — the rule does not regulate a prior activity but creates it.
critical_questions: Is the rule constitutive rather than merely regulative?
Were the rule's conditions actually satisfied in the required form?
Does the institution recognize the resulting status?
rule_and_precedent.example: Signing in front of two witnesses is what makes it a will.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from consistency of application
rule_and_precedent.definition: Relevantly like cases have been treated a certain way, therefore this case must be treated the same absent a stated distinction.
critical_questions: Are the comparison cases relevantly alike?
Was the prior treatment correct, or is it an error being propagated?
Has a general policy change been announced?
rule_and_precedent.example: Three earlier applicants with the same gap got waivers.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from negative implication
rule_and_precedent.definition: A rule lists certain items, therefore items not listed are excluded.
critical_questions: Is the list exhaustive or illustrative?
Was the omission deliberate or an oversight?
Does another provision cover the omitted item?
rule_and_precedent.example: The statute exempts hospitals and schools; clinics are not on the list.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from distinguishing a case
rule_and_precedent.definition: A cited precedent or analogy is set aside by identifying a difference material to its rationale.
critical_questions: Is the difference material to the reason the prior case came out as it did?
Would the distinction, if accepted, leave a coherent rule?
Is the distinction ad hoc — drawn only to escape this precedent?
rule_and_precedent.example: That ruling concerned a voluntary disclosure; this one was compelled.

rule_and_precedent.name: argument from custom
rule_and_precedent.definition: A settled, long-observed practice in a trade or community has normative force in the absence of a written rule.
critical_questions: Is the custom settled and generally observed, or occasional?
Do the parties belong to the community that observes it?
Does the custom conflict with a written rule or with fairness?
rule_and_precedent.example: In this trade, unsigned change orders have always been honored at the quoted rate.

rule_and_precedent.name: precedent slippery slope argument
rule_and_precedent.definition: Deciding this case a certain way would commit the decider, by consistency, to unacceptable decisions in later cases; therefore decide otherwise.
critical_questions: Is the later case really covered by the same rationale?
Can a principled stopping line be stated in advance?
Is the feared later case actually unacceptable?
rule_and_precedent.example: Grant this waiver and you cannot deny the next twenty on the same facts.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from commitment
dialectical_and_burden.definition: The other party is committed to proposition A by earlier statements or role; A implies B; therefore they must accept B.
critical_questions: Is the party really committed to A, and in the same sense?
Does A actually imply B?
Can the party retract A at acceptable cost?
dialectical_and_burden.example: You endorsed the same formula last year; it yields this number now.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from inconsistent commitment
dialectical_and_burden.definition: The other party holds two commitments that cannot both stand, therefore at least one must be abandoned.
critical_questions: Is the inconsistency real, or resolved by a distinction?
Are both commitments current?
Which commitment is the party more attached to, and does the argument's conclusion follow from dropping either?
dialectical_and_burden.example: You cannot both call the sample too small and cite its subgroup result.

dialectical_and_burden.name: reductio ad absurdum
dialectical_and_burden.definition: Assume the opponent's thesis, derive from it a contradiction or a plainly unacceptable consequence, conclude the thesis is false.
critical_questions: Does the derivation use only the opponent's premises plus agreed ones?
Is the derived consequence genuinely unacceptable to the opponent?
Which premise does the absurdity actually indict?
dialectical_and_burden.example: If every disputed vote must be recounted by hand, the certification deadline cannot be met at all.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from ignorance
dialectical_and_burden.definition: A has not been shown to be true despite a search where evidence would have appeared, therefore A may be presumed false (or vice versa).
critical_questions: Was the search thorough enough that evidence would have turned up?
Is this a domain with epistemic closure — a complete database, an exhaustive audit?
Where does the burden of proof lie?
dialectical_and_burden.example: The registry has no such license, and the registry is complete; there is no license.
dialectical_and_burden.caution: Legitimate only under a closed-world assumption; otherwise the appeal-to-ignorance fallacy.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from silence
dialectical_and_burden.definition: A source that would have mentioned A does not mention it, therefore A probably did not occur.
critical_questions: Would this source have had occasion and reason to mention A?
Is the source complete, or does it survive in fragments?
Are there conventions of omission in this genre of source?
dialectical_and_burden.example: The audited accounts list every transfer over ten thousand and show none that quarter.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from burden of proof
dialectical_and_burden.definition: The party asserting A bears the burden of establishing it; the burden has not been met; therefore A is not accepted.
critical_questions: Which party properly bears the burden in this kind of dispute?
What standard of proof applies?
Has the burden shifted through a prima facie showing?
dialectical_and_burden.example: The claim of prior use was never documented, so it fails on the record.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from presumption
dialectical_and_burden.definition: In the absence of sufficient evidence either way, a default position holds and the other side must displace it.
critical_questions: Is the default the right one for this forum and question?
What is the standard for rebutting it?
Has enough been offered to shift the presumption?
dialectical_and_burden.example: The instrument is presumed valid unless a defect is shown.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from a dilemma
dialectical_and_burden.definition: Two exhaustive alternatives each lead to the same conclusion, therefore the conclusion holds either way.
critical_questions: Are the horns exhaustive?
Does each horn really yield the stated conclusion?
Can one grasp a horn — accept it with its consequences?
dialectical_and_burden.example: Either the log was altered or the clock was wrong; either way the timestamp cannot be relied on.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from universalizability
dialectical_and_burden.definition: A judgment must hold for all relevantly similar cases including those where the arguer's own interests reverse, therefore test it by role reversal.
critical_questions: Are the cases relevantly similar under a stated criterion?
Would the arguer accept the judgment with the roles reversed?
Is there a principled asymmetry between the positions?
dialectical_and_burden.example: Would you accept this evidentiary standard if it were applied to your own filing?

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from gradualism
dialectical_and_burden.definition: Move the opponent from an accepted position to a contested one through a series of small, individually acceptable steps.
critical_questions: Is each step really small enough to follow from the last?
Does the cumulative move preserve the meaning of the original concession?
Where, if anywhere, should the opponent have stopped?
dialectical_and_burden.example: You accept disclosure at ten thousand; why not nine; why not eight?
dialectical_and_burden.caution: The engine behind sorites-style slopes; legitimate as a probe, abusive as a trap.

dialectical_and_burden.name: argument from concession
dialectical_and_burden.definition: Grant a point the opponent values in order to isolate the real point of disagreement and show the conclusion still stands.
critical_questions: Is the conceded point actually severable from the conclusion?
Does the concession cost more later than it buys now?
Is the remaining issue the one that decides the case?
dialectical_and_burden.example: Grant that the survey was well designed; it still cannot answer a question about causes.

attack_and_undercut.name: direct ad hominem
attack_and_undercut.definition: The arguer's character for honesty or judgment is attacked as a reason to discount their argument.
critical_questions: Is the character claim documented?
Is character relevant here — is the claim testimonial rather than demonstrative?
Would the argument stand on its own evidence regardless of who made it?
attack_and_undercut.example: He has twice been found to have falsified data, which bears on whether to take his unreplicated result on trust.
attack_and_undercut.caution: Legitimate only against source-based arguments; against a demonstration it is the abusive ad hominem fallacy.

attack_and_undercut.name: circumstantial ad hominem
attack_and_undercut.definition: The arguer's situation — employment, funding, membership — is cited as grounds to discount the argument.
critical_questions: Is the circumstance real and material to the claim?
Does the circumstance plausibly influence this particular judgment?
Is independent evidence for the claim available?
attack_and_undercut.example: The study finding no risk was funded by the manufacturer, which is a reason to look hard at the methods.

attack_and_undercut.name: bias ad hominem
attack_and_undercut.definition: An arguer is shown to have an interest that makes their testimony less credible than a disinterested source's.
critical_questions: What is the interest, and which way would it push the testimony?
Is the arguer presenting themselves as impartial?
Is the testimony corroborated by an uninterested source?
attack_and_undercut.example: She stands to receive the contract she is recommending.

attack_and_undercut.name: tu quoque
attack_and_undercut.definition: The arguer is shown not to practice what they argue for, undermining their standing or exposing an inconsistent commitment.
critical_questions: Does the inconsistency touch the claim's truth or only the arguer's standing?
Is the hypocrisy documented?
Could both the advice and the criticism of the adviser be correct?
attack_and_undercut.example: The auditor's own filings are late.
attack_and_undercut.caution: Only ever attacks credibility, never the argument's merits.

attack_and_undercut.name: poisoning the well
attack_and_undercut.definition: Adverse information about a source is introduced before the source speaks, so that anything said is discounted in advance.
critical_questions: Is the adverse information true and relevant?
Is it being used to prevent the argument from being heard at all?
Would the audience evaluate the evidence differently without the preface?
attack_and_undercut.example: Before the witness testifies, the jury hears that he has changed his story twice.
attack_and_undercut.caution: Sometimes a legitimate impeachment; abusive when preemptive and unrebuttable.

attack_and_undercut.name: impeachment by prior inconsistent statement
attack_and_undercut.definition: A source's present assertion is undermined by showing they earlier asserted the opposite.
critical_questions: Are the two statements really inconsistent, or context-dependent?
Has the source explained the change on the record?
Which statement was made closer to the events and under better conditions?
attack_and_undercut.example: In the deposition he put the meeting in April; today he says March.

attack_and_undercut.name: argument from motive
attack_and_undercut.definition: A party's motive to produce the claim is offered as a reason to suspect it.
critical_questions: Is the motive established rather than surmised?
Do people with this motive typically produce false claims of this kind?
Does motive explain the specific evidence, or only its existence?
attack_and_undercut.example: The complaint arrived the week after the termination.
attack_and_undercut.caution: Motive shows why someone might lie, never that they did.

attack_and_undercut.name: rebuttal by counterexample
attack_and_undercut.definition: A universal or generic claim is defeated by exhibiting an instance that falls under it and fails it.
critical_questions: Does the instance genuinely fall within the claim's scope?
Is the claim strictly universal or a defeasible generalization?
Is the counterexample real and correctly described?
attack_and_undercut.example: 'No open-source project sustains paid maintainers' — several do.

attack_and_undercut.name: undercutting defeater
attack_and_undercut.definition: Rather than denying the conclusion or a premise, the attack severs the link — showing that in these conditions the premises fail to support the conclusion.
critical_questions: What specific condition breaks the inference?
Is that condition present here?
Would the inference be restored if the condition were removed?
attack_and_undercut.example: The color reading is no evidence here, because the object is lit by sodium lamps.

attack_and_undercut.name: argument from an alternative explanation
attack_and_undercut.definition: An abductive argument is rebutted by presenting a rival hypothesis that accounts for the same evidence at least as well.
critical_questions: Does the rival explain all the evidence, not just part?
Is the rival independently plausible?
What observation would separate the two?
attack_and_undercut.example: The spike also follows from the reporting change made that month.

attack_and_undercut.name: argument from expert disagreement
attack_and_undercut.definition: Qualified experts in the field disagree about A, therefore the appeal to any one of them cannot settle A.
critical_questions: Is the disagreement among comparably qualified experts?
Is it about A itself or about a neighboring question?
Is one side's position marginal within the field?
attack_and_undercut.example: Two national panels reached opposite recommendations from the same trials.
attack_and_undercut.caution: Manufactured disagreement is the standard way to create false balance; check the weight, not just the existence, of dissent.
